title: Make Your Career Bloom
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Andrea Chiarelli argues that the real engine of career progression is not visible markers—titles, tenure, networks—but a deepening of cognitive complexity, and he maps that growth onto Bloom’s Revised Taxonomy. After noting Bloom’s original framework spanned cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains, he applies the six cognitive levels to professional development as a map from competence to leadership. Remember is the Foundation stage (mastering a field’s language, tools, and norms); Understand means grasping the “why” and contextualizing one’s work within the larger system; Apply is the Performance stage where others trust you to deliver; Analyse is where you stop executing within the system and begin to see it, tracing patterns and anticipating problems; Evaluate is discernment—weighing trade-offs and making judgment calls others seek out; and Create is generative leadership that builds new frameworks and shapes culture. Crucially, Chiarelli rejects a strict staircase reading: in practice professionals move between levels daily in a “deepening spiral,” and it is cognitive agility—deploying the right mode of thinking at the right moment—that distinguishes those who thrive. His central career claim is that people “arrive early” to leadership by thinking at the next level before they are given the title, and he closes with a concrete regimen: locate your current level, deliberately practice one verb from the next level, keep a learning log, and teach it to consolidate it.
points: The thesis relocates career growth from visible signals (titles, years, networks) to invisible cognitive depth—“the more complex the thinking, the greater the impact”—using Bloom’s taxonomy as a development map rather than a learning framework.

Chiarelli assigns each cognitive level a career identity—Remember/Foundation, Understand/Contextualise, Apply/Performance, Analyse/Strategise, Evaluate/Influence, Create/Leadership—giving professionals a vocabulary to locate themselves.

The pivotal transition is at Analyse, “the moment you cross from doing the work to improving it,” where you stop executing within the system and start seeing the system, tracing patterns and anticipating rather than reacting.

He explicitly rejects a linear staircase: real work is a “deepening spiral” in which one analyses, applies, and creates in the same day, so cognitive agility, not rigid progression, is what distinguishes those who lead.

The actionable engine of advancement is stretching into next-level thinking before the title arrives—the most effective professionals “arrive early” to leadership—supported by a four-step routine: locate yourself, stretch deliberately with one next-level verb, reflect via a learning log, and teach it.
quotes: It’s tempting to assume they’re more confident, better connected or simply luckier. More often, the real difference lies beneath the surface: it’s in how they think.
The six levels of cognition — from remembering information to creating new knowledge — describe remarkably well both how students learn and how professionals evolve.
Something shifts here. You stop just executing within the system and you begin to see the system.
This is analytical maturity: the moment you cross from doing the work to improving it.
Cognitive agility, not rigid progression, is what distinguishes those who lead and thrive.
they start thinking like leaders long before anyone gives them the title.
